rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni allows al-il to derive from governance, with wāw changed to yāʾ after a kasra; on this reading the offenders observe no policy, accommodation, or pledge toward believers.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون مأخوذا من آل يؤول إذا ساس، أبدل من الواو ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If al-il means covenant, it and dhimma are synonymous or near-synonymous; if al-il has another sense, the two words are distinct.
rows.anchor: من رأى أن الإل هو العهد جعله والذمة لفظين لمعنى واحد أو متقاربين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about pleasing believers by their mouths begins a new explanation: their outward manner contradicts their inward state, showing why their hearts will not keep the pact.
rows.anchor: واستأنف هذا الكلام أي: حالهم في الظاهر يخالف لباطنهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation is that they promise faith with their mouths while their hearts insist on unbelief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يرضونكم بأفواههم في العدة بالإيمان، وتأبى قلوبهم إلا الكفر.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they promise obedience while their hearts insist on disobedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يرضونكم في الطاعة، وتأبى قلوبهم إلا المعصية.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most remain ‘most’ rather than all because some are destined by God to believe.
rows.anchor: لأن منهم من قضى الله له بالإيمان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some retain good manners to protect their reputation and avoid disgrace, unlike the majority described as morally corrupt.
rows.anchor: لأن منهم من له حفظ لمراعاة الحال الحسنة من التعفف عما يثلم العرض

rows.speaker: ابن عطية والكرماني
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya and al-Kirmani explain ‘most of them are defiantly disobedient’ as meaning all of them are.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معنى وأكثرهم وكلهم فاسقون، قاله ابن عطية والكرماني.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority are so vicious that neither honor nor sound temperament restrains them from lies, schemes, and treachery; such conduct is condemned across religions, even by pre-Islamic Arabs who praised chastity, truth, fidelity, and good character.
rows.anchor: لا مروءة تردعهم، ولا طباع مرضية تزعهم، لا يحترزون عن كذب ولا مكر ولا خديعة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The default referent is the previously mentioned polytheists: they traded the Qurʾān and Islam for the small price of following desires after abandoning God’s religion.
rows.anchor: الظاهر عود الضمير على من قبله من المشركين المأمور بقتلهم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the people who traded God’s signs for a small price as Bedouins whom Abu Sufyan assembled for a meal.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هم الأعراب الذين جمعهم أبو سفيان على طعامه.

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih identifies them as a group of Jews and the signs as the Torah.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح: هم قوم من اليهود، وآيات الله التوراة.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies them as people of al-Taʾif who financed others to keep them from entering Islam.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هم أهل الطائف كانوا يمدون الناس بالأموال يمنعونهم من الدخول في الإسلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They turned others from His way’ means that they themselves turned away from God’s religion.
rows.anchor: فصدوا عن سبيله أي صرفوا أنفسهم عن دين الله وعدلوا عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent analysis makes sāʾa a verb on the pattern of biʾsa; it may instead remain an adjective with an understood object, meaning their deeds displeased them.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ساء هنا محولة إلى فعل. ومذ هو بابها مذهب بئس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning every believer clarifies that faith itself, rather than only the addressed believers, is the cause of their hostility; the people with these vices are transgressors in oppression, evil, and broken covenants.
rows.anchor: ولما كان قوله: لا يرقبوا فيكم يتوهم أن ذلك مخصوص بالمخاطبين، نبه على علة ذلك، وأن سبب المنافاة هو الإيمان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance here means abandoning unbelief and covenant-breaking and accepting Islam’s rulings; then they are brothers in religion.
rows.anchor: فإن تابوا عن الكفر ونقض العهد والتزموا أحكام الإسلام فإخوانكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that ikhwa means brothers by descent while ikhwan means friends is mistaken; both plurals can denote brothers by lineage or religion.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أن الإخوة تكون في النسب، والإخوان في الصداقة، فقد غلط.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The condition for religious brotherhood names all three duties, though the implied converse of the condition is apparently not intended.
rows.anchor: وعلق حصول الأخوة في الدين على الالتباس بمجموع الثلاثة، ويظهر أن مفهوم الشرط غير مراد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘We detail the signs for people who know’ is an explanatory parenthesis between the two conditional clauses, urging reflection on the rulings; only learned, understanding people consider them.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة اعتراض بين الشرطين، بين قوله: فإن تابوا، وقوله: وإن نكثوا، بعثا وتحريضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To taʿn the religion is to disparage or denigrate it, metaphorically extending the original sense of striking with a spear or similar object.
rows.anchor: وطعنوا: أي عابوه وثلبوه واستنقصوه. والطعن هنا مجاز، وأصله الإصابة بالرمح أو العود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fight the leaders of unbelief means its chiefs, singled out because they incite followers to remain unbelievers; the phrase can stand metonymically for fighting unbelievers.
rows.anchor: لأن من أسلم ثم ارتد فيكون قوله: فقاتلوا أئمة الكفر، أي رؤساء الكفر وزعماءه.

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani takes every unbeliever to be his own leader, so the command means to fight every unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقال الكرماني: كل كافر إمام نفسه، فالمعنى فقاتلوا كل كافر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes anyone who breaks the covenant and attacks the religion a leader among unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من أقدم على نكث العهد والطعن في الدين صار رأسا في الكفر، فهو من أئمة الكفر.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the leaders of unbelief as Quraysh’s chiefs.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أئمة الكفر زعماء قريش.

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi calls that identification remote because by the revelation of Surat Baraʾa Quraysh had been subdued, with only Muslims or those at peace remaining.
rows.anchor: وقال القرطبي: هو بعيد، لأن الآية في سورة براءة، وحين نزلت كان الله قد استأصل شأفة قريش

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada names Abu Jahl, ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, and others, but the author says this is weak unless meant only as examples because the verse came long after Badr.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: المراد أبو جهل بن هشام وعتبة بن ربيعة، وغيرهم، وهذا ضعيف إن لم يؤخذ على جهة المثال،

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa reportedly said these leaders had not yet disappeared and would keep arising and fighting.
rows.anchor: وروي عن حذيفة أنه قال: لم يجىء هؤلاء بعد، يريد لم ينقرضوا فهم يجيئون أبدا ويقاتلون.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya’s preferred reading is general: the command targets covenant-breaking unbelieving leaders in every age, with the Arab opponents of the Prophet first included and each generation having its own leaders.
rows.anchor: أصوب ما في هذا أن يقال: إنه لا يعنى بها معين، وإنما دفع الأمر بقتال أئمة الناكثين العهود

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the covenant as Islam: people first embraced Islam, then apostatized, broke their pledges, and attacked the religion, becoming leading unbelievers.
rows.anchor: كفروا بعد إسلامهم. ولذلك قرأ بعضهم: وإن نكثوا إيمانهم بالكسر، وهو قول الزمخشري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari explains the explicit label ‘leaders of unbelief’ in place of a pronoun as marking their preeminence in rebellion after reverting from Islam.
rows.anchor: فوضع أئمة الكفر موضع ضميرهم، إشعارا بأنهم إذا نكثوا في حالة الشرك تمردا وطغيانا

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The well-known Maliki position executes a protected non-Muslim who attacks the religion by denying the law or insulting the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والمشهور من مذهب مالك أن الذمي إذا طعن في الدين ففعل شيئا مثل تكذيب الشريعة والسب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ونحوه قتل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view disciplines a protected non-Muslim for publicly voicing familiar beliefs but executes him for blasphemy outside those beliefs, such as insulting the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن أعلن بشيء مما هو معهود من معتقده وكفره أدب على الإعلان وترك،

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa says such a person is invited to repent.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: يستتاب، واختلف إذا سب الذمي ثم أسلم تقية القتل.

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: The well-known Maliki view leaves a protected non-Muslim who insults the Prophet and then converts under threat alone, since Islam erases what preceded; the Utbiyya instead says to execute him.
rows.anchor: فالمشهور من مذهب مالك أنه يترك، لأن الإسلام يجب ما قبله، وفي العتبية أنه يقتل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second hamza in aʾimma is eased to yāʾ by the Two Haramis and Abu ʿAmr; other transmitters preserve two hamzas, Hisham inserts an alif, and the form derives from aʾimma, plural of imam, with assimilated mīm.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحرميان وأبو عمرو: بإبدال الهمزة الثانية ياء. وروي عن نافع مد الهمزة.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari describes the hamza as articulated between hamza and yāʾ; he rejects explicit yāʾ, but Abu Hayyan defends the recognized two-hamza reading and rebukes his disparagement of leading reciters.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: (فإن قلت) : كيف لفظ أئمة؟ (قلت) : همزة بعدها همزة بين بين، أي بين مخرج الهمزة والياء.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They have no oaths’ means either that they do not keep their oaths or that an omitted qualifier means they have no oaths they will honor.
rows.anchor: ونفى إيمانهم لما لم يثبتوا عليها ولا وفوا بها جعلوا لا أيمان لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers use fatḥa in aymān; al-Hasan, ʿAta, Zayd ibn ʿAli, and Ibn ʿAmir read kasra, meaning no faith or Islam, though Abu ʿAli calls this weak and repetitive.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: بفتح الهمزة. وقرأ الحسن، وعطاء، وزيد بن علي، وابن عامر: لا إيمان لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan argues that kasra can mean no protection or safe conduct for the People of the Book after apostasy and breach; Abu Hatim and al-Zamakhshari report al-Hasan’s gloss as no Islam.
rows.anchor: فالوجه في كسر الألف أنه مصدر أمنه إيمانا، ومنه قوله تعالى: وآمنهم من خوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa uses the fatḥa reading to argue that an unbeliever’s oath is not binding; al-Shafiʿi says it is binding and means they fail to keep it, as shown by the verse’s charge of breach.
rows.anchor: وبقراءة الفتح استشهد أبو حنيفة على أن يمين الكافر لا يكون يمينا وعند الشافعي يمينهم يمين، وقال: معناه أنهم لا يوفون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The aim in fighting them is that they desist from their wrongdoing; Abu Hayyan reads this as God’s generosity and mercy even toward the offender.
rows.anchor: لعلهم ينتهون متعلق بقوله: فقاتلوا أئمة الكفر، أي ليكن غرضكم في مقاتلتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle alā is an exhortation urging combat; al-Zamakhshari analyzes it as a question over the absence of fighting, used for emphatic encouragement.
rows.anchor: ألا حرف عرض، ومعناه هنا الحض على قتالهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives three reasons for fighting, each independently enough to urge it: breaking pledges, plotting to expel the Messenger, and initiating hostilities.
rows.anchor: وهو ثلاثة أشياء جمعوها، وكل واحد منها على انفراده كاف في الحض على مقاتلتهم.

rows.speaker: السدي وابن إسحاق والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Kalbi say the verse concerns Meccan unbelievers who broke Hudaybiyya’s treaty and helped Banu Bakr against Khuzaʿa.
rows.anchor: قال السدي، وابن إسحاق، والكلبي: نزلت في كفار مكة، نكثوا أيمانهم بعد عهد الحديبية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The planned expulsion is variously identified as Quraysh’s Dar al-Nadwa plot against the Prophet, Banu Bakr’s plot against him in Medina, or Jewish treachery and assistance to hypocrites; al-Hasan specifies Medina.
rows.anchor: وهمهم هو هم قريش بإخراج الرسول من مكة حين تشاوروا بدار الندوة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya finds the Jews a fitting referent for initiating hostilities at Uhud and the Confederates: they first received the clear Book and challenge, then resorted to fighting when unable to answer it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا مستقيم لغزوة أحد والأحزاب وغيرهما، وهم الذين كانت منهم البداءة بالمقاتلة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya argues that the first aggressor is more unjust and asks why believers should not meet the enemy with comparable force.
rows.anchor: فعدلوا عن المعارضة لعجزهم عنها إلى القتال، فهم البادئون، والبادئ أظلم،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Quraysh first breached the pact by aiding their allies Banu Bakr against the Prophet’s allies Khuzaʿa; al-Tabari instead identifies the first act as Badr.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ما بدأت به قريش من معونة بني بكر حلفائهم على خزاعة حلفاء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads badawkum without hamza, explained by easing the hamza of badaʾa to yāʾ and then dropping it before the plural wāw, as in ramaytum to ramawkum.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: بدوكم بغير همز، ووجهه أنه سهل الهمزة من بدأت بإبدالها ياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Do you fear them?’ rebukes fear of the enemy; God has greater right to be feared, so believers should kill His enemies.
rows.anchor: أتخشونهم تقرير للخشية منهم، وتوبيخ عليها. فالله أحق أن تخشوه فتقتلوا أعداءه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase an takhshawhu has several grammatical analyses: apposition to Allah in the nominative, an oblique or accusative phrase with an omitted preposition, Abu al-Baqa’s subject analysis, or Ibn Atiyya’s predicate analysis; Sībawayh permits the indefinite comparative predicate.
rows.anchor: وأن تخشوه بدل من الله أي: وخشية الله أحق من خشيتهم وأن تخشوه في موضع رفع،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes ‘if you are believers’ to mean that sound faith entails fearing only the Lord and not caring about others, as in 33:39.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يعني أن قضية الإيمان الصحيح أن لا يخشى المؤمن إلا ربه ولا يبالي بمن سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threatened punishment at believers’ hands is worldly killing, capture, and plunder; these promises strengthened their hearts and intentions.
rows.anchor: وتعذيبهم بأيدي المؤمنين هو في الدنيا بالقتل والأسر والنهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their humiliation means abasement, and victory means subduing them; believers’ chests are healed by God’s religion being exalted and unbelievers being punished and humiliated.
rows.anchor: وخزيهم هو إهانتهم وذلهم، وينصركم يظفركم بهم، وشفاء الصدور بإعلاء دين الله وتعذيب الكفار وخزيهم.

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads the verb ‘we heal’ with nūn, shifting the address by grammatical turn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: ونشف بالنون على الالتفات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘The chests of a believing people’ generalizes the promise to every believer; another view limits it to a particular group.
rows.anchor: وجاء التركيب صدور قوم مؤمنين ليشمل المخاطبين وكل مؤمن، لأن ما يصيب أهل الكفر من العذاب والخزي هو شفاء لصدر كل مؤمن.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the people as Yemeni and Sabaean groups who came to Mecca, converted, suffered abuse, and complained to the Prophet, who promised relief soon.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هم بطون من اليمن وسبأ قدموا مكة فأسلموا، فلقوا من أهلها أذى شديدا،

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Suddi identify them as Khuzaʿa, many of whom were believers and had been harmed in the broken pact and ensuing war; a Khuzaʿi poem recalls their submission and being killed at prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد والسدي: هم خزاعة. ووجه تخصيصهم أنهم هم الذين نقض فيهم العهد ونالتهم الحرب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Removing rancor restates the healing of believers’ chests; readings make yudhhib either intransitive with ghayẓ as its subject or similarly with a variant case ending.
rows.anchor: وهذه الجملة كالتأكيد للتي قبلها، لأن شفاء الصدر من آلة الغيظ هو إذهاب الغيظ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fulfilled promises proved the Prophet’s truth; the sequence begins with enemy suffering, then Muslim victory, then believers’ relief and recovered vengeance, emphasizing Arab zeal for defeating enemies rather than spoils and food.
rows.anchor: وهذه المواعيد كلها وجدت، فكان ذلك دليلا على صدق الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وصحة نبوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers raise yatūbu as a new statement that some Meccans and others will repent, which many later did sincerely.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ويتوب الله رفعا، وهو استئناف إخبار بأن بعض أهل مكة وغيرهم يتوب عن كفره،

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج وأبو الفتح
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ, al-Zajjaj, and Abu al-Fath argue that repentance occurs whether the unbelievers are fought or not, so it should not be included in the command’s result.
rows.anchor: وهذا أمر موجود سواء قوتلوا أو لم يقاتلوا، فلا وجه لإدخال اليوم في جواب الشرط الذي في قاتلوهم

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي والأعرج وابن أبي إسحاق وعيسى الثقفي وعمرو بن عبيد وعمر بن قائد وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: These readers put yatūba in the subjunctive, linking repentance to the command’s consequence by meaning.
rows.anchor: ويعقوب فيما روي عنهما: ويتوب الله بنصب الباء، جعله داخلا في جواب الأمر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the subjunctive works if the believers’ fighting is itself their repentance and completion of faith.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ويتوجه ذلك عندي إذا ذهب إلى أن التوبة يراد بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations connect repentance to overcoming reluctance to fight, or to newly lawful wealth prompting repentance from earlier unlawful gains.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: لما أمرهم بالمقاتلة شق ذلك على بعضهم، فإذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers taking ‘whom He wills’ as unbelievers: fighting and Muslim victory can lead many to Islam, whether from conviction or initial compulsion, as happened at Mecca; Abdullah ibn Abi Sarh later became an exemplary Companion.
rows.anchor: والذي يظهر أن ذلك بالنسبة إلى الكفار، فالمعنى على من يشاء من الكفار، وذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows what will happen as He knows what has happened, assuring that the promised outcomes will certainly occur; He is wise in moving servants from one state to another.
rows.anchor: والله عليم يعلم ما سيكون مثل ما يعلم ما قد كان، وفي ذلك تقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers will not be left as they are until the sincere are distinguished: those who fight for God and take no confidant outside God, His Messenger, and the believers.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنكم لا تتركون على ما أنتم عليه حتى يتبين الخلص منكم وهم المجاهدون في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘They did not take an intimate ally’ coordinates with ‘they fought’; walīja derives from walaja, like dakhīla from dakhala, and means an inner-circle confidant or secret entrant, hence its resemblance to hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: ولم يتخذوا معطوف على جاهدوا. غير متخذين وليجة، والوليجة فعيلة من ولج كالدخيلة من دخل، وهي البطانة.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses walīja as treachery.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الوليجة الخيانة. وقال

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses walīja as deception.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الخديعة. وقال عطاء:

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAta glosses walīja as close friends.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء: الأوداء. وقال الحسن:

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan glosses walīja as unbelief and hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الكفر والنفاق. وقال أبو عبيدة:

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda defines walīja broadly as anything inserted into something to which it does not belong, including a person among a group who is not one of them; the form is unchanged for singular, dual, and plural.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: كل شيء أدخلته في شيء وليس منه فهو وليجة، والرجل يكون في القوم وليس منهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse censures hypocrites for adopting secret allies, especially when fighting is prescribed; believers must be tested because a hypocrite can fight, so jihad must be sincere and free of hypocrisy, ostentation, and ingratiating oneself with unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية طعن على المنافقين الذين اتخذوا الولائج لا سيما عند فرض القتال،

rows.speaker: الحسن ويعقوب وسلام
rows.claim: The majority read the closing address with tāʾ; al-Hasan, Yaʿqub in one transmission, and Salam read it with yāʾ, shifting to third person.
rows.anchor: والله خبير بما تعملون قرأ الجمهور بالتاء على الخطاب مناسبة لقوله: أم حسبتم. وقرأ الحسن ويعقوب في رواية رويس وسلام بالياء

rows.speaker: ابن السميفع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfi reads the phrase as ‘that they assist in its maintenance,’ with a passive/causative construction.
rows.anchor: ابن السميفع: أن يعمروا بضم الياء وكسر الميم، أن يعينوا على عمارته.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and al-Jahdari read the noun ‘mosque’ in the singular; the other seven readers and named early readers use the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير، وأبو عمرو، والجحدري: مسجد بالإفراد، وباقي السبعة ومجاهد وقتادة وأبو جعفر والأعرج وشيبة بالجمع.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse follows the disavowal of polytheists and their blameworthy deeds: they had claimed virtues, especially maintaining the Sacred Mosque, as grounds to escape that disavowal.
rows.anchor: ومناسبة هذه الآية لما قبلها أنه تعالى لما ذكر البراءة من المشركين وأنواعا من قبائحهم توجب البراءة منهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that after Badr the emigrants and Helpers taunted prisoners; after Ali rebuked al-ʿAbbas and the Prophet mentioned kinship, al-ʿAbbas claimed virtues of mosque maintenance, Kaʿba custody, watering pilgrims, and ransoming captives, prompting this reply.
rows.anchor: روي أنه أقبل المهاجرون والأنصار على أسارى بدر يعيرونهم بالشرك، وطفق علي يوبخ العباس، فقال الرسول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘It was not for polytheists’ means it was not rightfully theirs, although they maintained the sanctuary in practice by dominance; al-Zamakhshari glosses it as neither proper nor sound.
rows.anchor: ومعنى ما كان للمشركين: أي بالحق الواجب، وإلا فقد عمروه قديما وحديثا على سبيل التغلب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosque maintenance may mean frequent attendance, raising or repairing the structure, worship, circumambulation, or prayer.
rows.anchor: وعمارته وحوله والقعود فيه والمكث من قولهم: فلان يعمر المسجد أي يكثر غشيانه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For singular masjid, the referent may be the Sacred Mosque or mosque-kind generally with the Haram as its chief; for plural masājid, it may denote the Haram as all its parts or as qibla and leader of mosques, or genuinely include every mosque for rhetorical emphasis.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالإفراد فيحتمل أن يراد به المسجد الحرام لقوله: وعمارة المسجد الحرام أو الجنس فيدخل تحته المسجد الحرام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shāhidīn is an accusative circumstantial phrase: it is incoherent to combine maintaining God’s sanctuaries with unbelief in Him and His worship.
rows.anchor: وانتصب شاهدين على الحال، والمعنى: ما استقام لهم أن يجمعوا بين أمرين متنافيين

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAli reads shāhidūn with an understood subject pronoun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: شاهدون على إضمارهم شاهدون،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their testimony against themselves is variously their polytheist talbiya during circumambulation, their stated worship of al-Lat and al-ʿUzza, denial of the Messenger, self-identification as polytheists, or visible pagan rites such as idols and naked circumambulation.
rows.anchor: وشهادتهم على أنفسهم بالكفر قولهم في الطواف: لبيك لبيك لا شريك لك، إلا شريكا هو لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative takes ‘themselves’ to mean their messengers, since every Arab clan descended from them; a reading with fatḥa on fāʾ is cited in support, meaning their most eminent members.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه شاهدين على رسولهم، وأطلق عليه أنفسهم لأنه ما من بطن من بطون العرب إلا وله فيهم ولادة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their earlier good works—mosque maintenance, custody, watering, freeing captives, and the like—are nullified.
rows.anchor: أولئك حبطت أعمالهم التي هي العمارة والحجابة والسقاية وفك العناة وغيرها مما ذكر أنه من الأعمال الحميدة.

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari argues that if unbelief or a grave sin erases sound works that precede it, it is even more obvious that simultaneous unbelief invalidates them; the circumstantial ‘bearing witness’ shows simultaneity.
rows.anchor: وإذا هدم الكفر أو الكبيرة الأعمال الثابتة الصحيحة إذا تعقبها، فما ظنك بالمقارن؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan calls al-Zamakhshari’s reference to a grave sin an Muʿtazilite insinuation, since they hold that major sins cancel deeds.
rows.anchor: وقوله: أو الكبيرة، دسيسة اعتزال لأن الكبيرة عندهم من المعاصي تحبط الأعمال.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse states the polytheists’ final fate as permanent Hell; Zayd reads the phrase with yāʾ and the accusative as a circumstantial expression while ‘in the Fire’ is the predicate.
rows.anchor: وفي النار هم خالدون ذكر مآل المشركين وهو النار خالدين فيها.

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi infers that unbelievers may not maintain Muslim mosques, their building bequests are invalid, and they should be barred from mosques; entry without permission merits taʿzir, though permission removes that penalty and exclusion is preferable.
rows.anchor: وقال الواحدي: دلت الآية على أن الكفار ممنوعون من عمارة مسجد المسلمين، ولو أوصى لم تقبل وصيته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author notes counterexamples: the Prophet lodged the non-Muslim Thaqif delegation in the mosque and tied Thumama ibn Athal there while he was an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقد أنزل رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وفد ثقيف وهم كفار المسجد، وربط ثمامة بن أثال الحنفي في سارية

rows.speaker: الجحدري وحماد بن أبي سلمة عن ابن كثير
rows.claim: Al-Jahdari and Hammad ibn Abi Salama from Ibn Kathir read ‘a mosque for God’ in the singular; the seven readers and others read the plural.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجحدري، وحماد بن أبي سلمة عن ابن كثير: مسجدا لله بالتوحيد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rightful mosque maintenance includes repair, cleaning, lighting, reverence, regular attendance for worship and remembrance, especially study of knowledge, while avoiding worldly chatter.
rows.anchor: ويتناول عمارتها رم ما تهدم منها، وتنظيفها، وتنويرها، وتعظيمها، واعتيادها للعبادة والذكر.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says to bear witness to the faith of someone who regularly attends a mosque.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: «إذا رأيتم الرجل يعتاد المسجد فاشهدوا له بالإيمان»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits belief in the Messenger because belief in the afterlife comes from prophetic reports, because belief in God is conventionally paired with belief in the Messenger, or because prayer and zakat are learned from him.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر الإيمان بالرسول، لأن الإيمان باليوم الآخر إنما هو متلقف من أخبار الرسول،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosques are built as communal places for prayer and worship, including remembrance and retreat; zakat is paired with mosque maintenance because the community makes contributors and eligible recipients visible.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من بناء المساجد وعمارتها هو كونها مجتمعا لإقامة الصلوات فيها والتعبدات

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says ‘fears none but God’ means fear in reverence, worship, and obedience, while ordinary worldly apprehensions remain possible.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: يريد خشية التعظيم والعبادة والطاعة، ولا محالة أن الإنسان يخشى غيره،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari reads the fear as piety in worldly affairs: when God’s right conflicts with one’s own, prefer God’s pleasure; another view contrasts fear of God with the pagans’ fear and hope in idols.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هي الخشية والتقوى في أبواب الدنيا، وأن لا يختار على رضا الله رضا غيره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s ‘perhaps’ is certain wherever it occurs in the Qurʾan; the wording denies polytheists any grounds for presuming guidance and favors fear over hope, warning that good works may be corrupted unnoticed.
rows.anchor: وعسى من الله تعالى واجب حيثما وقعت في القرآن، وفي ذلك قطع أطماع المشركين أن يكونوا مهتدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase ‘among the guided’ makes their guidance a qualified membership in that honored group rather than an unqualified declaration of guidance.
rows.anchor: وقال تعالى: أن يكونوا من المهتدين، أي: من الذين سبقت لهم الهداية ولم يأت التركيب إن يكونوا مهتدين،

rows.speaker: النعمان بن بشير
rows.claim: In the report in Sahih Muslim, men at the Prophet’s pulpit disputed whether watering pilgrims, maintaining the Sacred Mosque, or jihad was best; Umar silenced them and the verse was revealed after he promised to ask the Prophet.
rows.anchor: في صحيح مسلم من حديث النعمان بن بشير قال: كنت عند منبر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال رجل: ما أبالي أن لا أعمل عملا بعد أن أسقي الحاج.

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya records other occasions of revelation, all involving people boasting about watering pilgrims and maintaining the sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وذكر ابن عطية وقوله أقوالا أخر في سبب النزول كلها تدل على الافتخار بالسقاية والعمارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common readings sِqāya and ʿimāra are verbal nouns treated as concrete people or deeds, requiring an omitted ‘people of’ before the first or ‘deed of’ before the second.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: سقاية وعمارة وهما مصدران نحو الصيانة والوقاية وقوبلا بالذوات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Baqir, and Abu Haywa read ‘waterers of pilgrims’ and ‘custodians of the mosque’; Ibn Jubayr similarly reads them as plurals with the mosque accusative, and al-Dahhak has a variant vocalization and plural pattern.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن الزبير والباقر وأبو حيوة: سقاة الحاج، وعمرة المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The watering service belonged to Banu Hashim and was overseen by al-ʿAbbas; after revelation he thought of giving it up, but the Prophet told him to continue because it was better for his family.
rows.anchor: وكانت السقاية في بني هاشم وكان العباس يتولاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Custodianship belonged to Banu ʿAbd al-Dar; after the Prophet gave the Kaʿba key to Shayba and ʿUthman ibn Talha on the eighth day of the conquest, he declared it theirs in perpetuity and only an unjust person would contest it.
rows.anchor: وعمارة المسجد هي السدانة، وكانت في بني عبد الدار،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse rejects equating polytheists and their invalidated deeds with believers and their accepted deeds; unbelievers wronged themselves by rejecting faith and wronged the sanctuary by making it a place for idols.
rows.anchor: إنكار أن يشبه المشركون بالمؤمنين وأعمالهم المحبطة بأعمالهم المثبتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast links the believers’ hoped-for guidance in the prior verse with God’s denial of guidance to the oppressive polytheists.
rows.anchor: وذكر في المؤمنين إثبات الهداية لهم بقوله: فعسى أولئك أن يكونوا من المهتدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who purify themselves from shirk, migrate from their homeland, and risk wealth and life in jihad rank above those boasting of sanctuary service.
rows.anchor: فطهروا أنفسهم من دنس الشرك بالإيمان، وطهروا أبدانهم بالهجرة إلى موطن الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Greater in rank’ may be a true comparative assuming the polytheists’ service had merit, or comparing these believers with those who neither migrated nor fought; another view takes ‘greater’ simply to mean great.
rows.anchor: وأعظم هنا يسوغ أن تبقى على بابها من التفضيل، ويكون ذلك على تقدير اعتقاد المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘With God’ denotes rank and standing, not physical place.
rows.anchor: وعند الله بالمكانة لا بالمكان

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi offers a mystical account: purified human spirits shine with divine majesty and beauty and rise from servitude to nearness; Abu Hayyan says it resembles Sufi speech.
rows.anchor: الأرواح المقدسة البشرية إذا تطهرت عن دنس الأوصاف البدنية والقاذورات الجسدانية أشرقت بأنوار الجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers’ three qualities—faith, migration, and striving with life and wealth—are matched with mercy, divine approval, and Gardens; mercy is first as the broadest blessing, approval next as the highest aim, and Gardens complete the reward.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت الأوصاف التي تحلوا بها وصاروا بها عبيده حقيقة هي ثلاثة: الإيمان، والهجرة، والجهاد بالمال والنفس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s approval precedes the Gardens because His being pleased with a servant is better than dwelling in Paradise, as in the authentic report where God promises never to be displeased with its people.
rows.anchor: وقدم على الجنات لأن رضا الله عن العبد أفضل من إسكانهم الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Everlasting Gardens repay migration: believers left their prosperous homelands for the abode of faith and revelation and receive enduring bliss; the recompense sequence proceeds from general mercy to the noblest reward to completion.
rows.anchor: وهذا مقابل لقوله «وهاجروا» لأنهم تركوا أوطانهم التي نشأوا فيها وكانوا فيها منعمين،

rows.speaker: التبريزي
rows.claim: Al-Tabrizi says the indefinite ‘mercy’ and ‘approval’ magnify the blessings beyond description.
rows.anchor: قال التبريزي: ونكر الرحمة والرضوان للتفخيم والتعظيم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash, Talha ibn Musarrif, and Humayd ibn Hilal read yubashshiruhum with light shīn; Abu Bakr from ʿAsim has ḍamma on the rāʾ of riḍwān; al-Aʿmash adds ḍamma on rāʾ and ḍād, which Abu Hatim rejects but Abu Hayyan allows by Arabic analogy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش، وطلحة بن مصرف، وحميد بن هلال: يبشرهم بفتح الياء وضم الشين خفيفة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the conquest of Mecca, converts were told their faith was incomplete until they migrated and broke loyalties with unbelieving kin; after complaining that this would destroy family ties, livelihoods, and homes, they migrated and refused even aid or shelter to relatives, before later receiving a concession.
rows.anchor: كان قبل فتح مكة من آمن لم يتم إيمانه إلا بأن يهاجر ويصادم أقاربه الكفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited battle locations include Badr, Qurayza and Nadir, Hudaybiya, Khaybar, and the conquest of Mecca; historians and battle scholars count about eighty such occasions.
rows.anchor: وهذه المواطن: وقعات بدر، وقريظة والنضير، والحديبية، وخيبر، وفتح مكة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hunayn is a valley between Mecca and al-Taʾif near Dhu al-Majaz; it is declined as a place name, and the coordination with ‘day’ joins a time to a place, with grammarians differing over the omitted preposition.
rows.anchor: وحنين واد بين مكة والطائف قريب من ذي المجاز

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: The amazement at the army’s size is attributed to one speaker despite being assigned to all; Ibn al-Musayyib identifies the speaker variously as Abu Bakr, Salama ibn Salama, Ibn Abbas, or a man of Banu Bakr.
rows.anchor: وإذ بدل من يوم وأضاف الإعجاب إلى جميعهم، وإن كان صادرا من واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet disliked the boast that the Muslims could not be defeated because of their numbers, and they were left to its consequence.
rows.anchor: ونقل أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ساءه كلام هذا القائل، ووكلوا إلى كلام الرجل.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reported Muslim numbers at Hunayn are sixteen thousand from Ibn Abbas, fourteen thousand from al-Nahhas, twelve thousand from Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Ishaq, and al-Waqidi, or eleven thousand five hundred from Muqatil via Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وهذه الكثرة عن ابن عباس ستة عشر ألفا، وعن النحاس أربعة عشر ألفا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘the earth seemed narrow despite its breadth,’ bāʾ is circumstantial and mā is infinitive: fear made the spacious earth feel too constricted to offer escape; raḥb means width, with Zayd ibn ʿAli reading the hāʾ unvocalized in the Tamim dialect.
rows.anchor: والباء في بما رحبت للحال، وما مصدرية أي:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Then you turned away fleeing’ is grammatically assigned to all although many heroes remained with the Prophet; the narrative says he brought ten thousand to Mecca, gained two thousand pardoned men, and faced a coalition of Hawazin, Thaqif, and other tribes numbering thirty thousand, who ambushed the Muslims at Hunayn.
rows.anchor: ثم وليتم مدبرين أي: وليتم فارين على أدباركم منهزمين تاركين رسول الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says some Meccan converts who had been pardoned fled toward Mecca hoping to cause a Muslim rout.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: ويقال إن الطلقاء من أهل مكة فروا وقصدوا إلقاء الهزيمة في المسلمين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet held his ground on the gray mule Duldul; al-Abbas held its bridle, with relatives and companions around him, while ten men remained, including Abu Bakr and Umar; Abbas’s poem praises their steadfastness.
rows.anchor: على بغلة شهباء تسمى دلدل لا يتخلخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Umm Sulaym stood holding Abu Talha’s camel with a dagger; the Prophet dismounted, prayed for help, threw dirt and pebbles at the enemy, and said ‘May the faces be ruined’; a report says every Hawazini got dirt in his eyes.
rows.anchor: وثبتت أم سليم في جملة من ثبت ممسكة بعيرا لأبي طلحة وفي يدها خنجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Prophet’s order, al-Abbas called the companions of the tree and Surat al-Baqara; the Helpers rallied together answering ‘Here we are,’ and the enemy fled.
rows.anchor: ناد أصحاب السمرة، فنادى الأنصار فخذا فخذا، ثم نادى يا أصحاب الشجرة، يا أصحاب سورة البقرة،

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: In Sahih Muslim’s report from al-Baraʾ, Hawazin archers loosed a volley like a swarm of locusts, scattering the Muslims before they rallied to the Prophet, who dismounted and prayed for victory.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح مسلم من حديث البراء: أن هوازن كانوا رماة فرموهم برشق من نبل كأنها رجل من جراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet declared that the fighting had become intense and pursued the defeated enemy on his mule.
rows.anchor: فقال: «هذا حين حمي الوطيس» وركض رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم خلفهم على بغلته.

rows.speaker: أبو جرول زهير بن صرد الجشمي
rows.claim: Abu Jarwal Zuhayr ibn Sard, a Hawazin captive at Hunayn, sat before the Prophet as he divided the captives and reminded him of his upbringing and nursing among Hawazin before reciting a plea in verse.
rows.anchor: قال: لما كان يوم حنين أسرنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فبينا هو يميز بين الرجال والنساء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion of revelation followed Ali’s proclamation at Mecca that the treaty with polytheists was repudiated, when people feared hardship, closed roads, and loss of transport; another followed worry about losing food trade after polytheists were called impure.
rows.anchor: لما أمر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم عليا أن يقرأ على مشركي مكة أول براءة، وينبذ إليهم عهدهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars use ‘polytheist’ for one who associates another deity with God and do not classify People of the Book as polytheists; others include them under shirk as a term for disbelief.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن المشرك من اتخذ مع الله إلها آخر، وعلى أن أهل الكتاب ليسوا بمشركين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read najas with fatḥa as an impurity noun; the apparent sense calls the polytheists impure or possessors of impurity.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: نجس بفتح النون والجيم، وهو مصدر نجس نجسا أي قذر قذرا،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وعمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz say shirk makes the people themselves physically impure, like wine, dogs, and pigs; al-Hasan also requires ablution after touching a polytheist, a position accepted only by al-Hadi among Zaydis.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، والحسن، وعمر بن عبد العزيز، وغيره: الشرك هو الذي نجسهم، فأعيانهم نجسة كالخمر والكلاب

rows.speaker: قتادة ومعمر بن راشد
rows.claim: Qatada, Maʿmar, and others explain the impurity as major ritual impurity because their washing after intercourse is invalid; Malik therefore requires a convert to perform ghusl, whereas Ibn Abd al-Hakam does not.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة، ومعمر بن راشد وغيرهما: وصف المشرك بالنجاسة لأنه جنب، إذ غسله من الجنابة ليس بغسل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them impure may be an emphatic description because they do not purify or bathe and do not avoid filth.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أنهم لا يتطهرون ولا يغتسلون ولا يجتنبون النجاسات، فجعلوا نجسا مبالغة في وصفهم بالنجاسة.

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة وابن السميفع
rows.claim: Abu Haywa reads najis with kasra and a shortened active-participle form, while Ibn al-Sumayfi reads anjās, which can be a plural of the verbal noun or adjective.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: نجس بكسر النون وسكون الجيم على تقدير حذف الموصوف،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on approach prevents Muslims from allowing polytheists to enter or circumambulate the Sacred Mosque for pilgrimage, umrah, or otherwise, as they had done in the pre-Islamic period.
rows.anchor: وفي النهي عن القربان منعهم عن دخوله والطواف به بحج أو عمرة أو غير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Those who were given the Book’ explains the referent of ‘those’; the verse explicitly covers Jews and Romans, and scholars agree that jizya is also taken from Magians, reportedly followers of the prophet Zaradusht.
rows.anchor: من الذين أوتوا الكتاب بيان لقوله: الذين. والظاهر اختصاص أخذ الجزية من أهل الكتاب وهم بنو إسرائيل والروم نصا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maliki scholars differ about Arab Magians; the majority treats Samaritans and Sabians as Jews or Christians, taking jizya and accepting their slaughtered food, while other opinions reject both or accept jizya but not their food.
rows.anchor: واختلف أصحاب مالك في مجوس العرب. وأما السامرة والصابئة فالجمهور على أنهم من اليهود والنصارى تؤخذ منهم الجزية

rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Awzaʿi permits jizya from every worshipper of idols or fire and every denier.
rows.anchor: وقال الأوزاعي: تؤخذ من كل عابد وثن أو نار أو جاحد مكذب.

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa offers Arab polytheists only Islam or the sword but accepts jizya from People of the Book and other non-Arab unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة: لا يقبل من مشركي العرب إلا الإسلام أو السيف، وتقبل من أهل الكتاب ومن سائر كفار العجم الجزية.

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik takes jizya from fire-worshippers, idolaters, and others of any ethnicity, including Arab Taghlibis and Quraysh, except apostates.
rows.anchor: وقال مالك: تؤخذ من عابد النار والوثن وغير ذلك كائنا من كان من عربي تغلبي أو قرشي أو عجمي إلا المرتد.

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأحمد وأبو ثور
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr limit jizya to Jews, Christians, and Magians.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي، وأحمد، وأبو ثور: لا تقبل إلا من اليهود والنصارى والمجوس فقط.

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة ومالك والشافعي
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafiʿi assess the tax only on free, adult, sane men, excluding reclusive monks; Malik keeps an existing assessment on monks who later withdraw and assesses church monks, while the status of elderly men is disputed.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة ومالك والشافعي: لا تؤخذ إلا من الرجال البالغين الأحرار العقلاء، ولا تضرب على رهبان الديارات والصوامع المنقطعين.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse itself specifies neither the per-person amount nor the payment date.
rows.anchor: ولم تتعرض الآية لمقدار ما على كل رأس ولا لوقت إعطائها

rows.speaker: مالك والثوري والشافعي وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Rates differ: Malik and many scholars use Umar’s four dinars for gold or forty dirhams for silver plus provisions and clothing; al-Thawri says Umar varied rates by means; al-Shafiʿi sets one dinar; Abu Hanifa sets 12, 24, or 48 dirhams by means and exempts a nonworking poor person.
rows.anchor: فذهب مالك وكثير من أهل العلم إلى ما فرضه عمر: أربعة دنانير على أهل الذهب، وأربعون درهما على أهل الفضة،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says the listed rates concern the interim period; a negotiated settlement may be any amount, and Abu Hanifa assesses payment at the start of a year while al-Shafiʿi does so at its end.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وهذا كله في الفترة. وأما الصلح فهو ما صولحوا عليه من قليل أو كثير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jizya derives from jazāʾ, compensation for a benefit: it is payment in exchange for the security granted, with a cited verse of poetry illustrating the root.
rows.anchor: وسميت جزية من جزى يجزي إذا كافأ عما أسدي عليه، فكأنهم أعطوها جزاء ما منحوا من الأمن،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets ‘by hand’ as paying directly in person rather than sending payment through another.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعطونها بأيديهم ولا يرسلون بها.

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: Uthman says payment is made in cash, not deferred.
rows.anchor: وقال عثمان: يعطونها نقدا لا نسيئة.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes the payer’s hand to be below the collector’s, indicating subordination.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: يعطونها وأيديهم تحت يد الآخذ، فالمعنى أنهم مستعلى عليهم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings of ‘by hand’ are acknowledgment, your power and coercive authority, a favor of granting them protection, voluntary initial giving, payment by the community as a whole without elite exemption, or wealth and ability excluding the poor.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عن اعتراف. وقيل: عن قوة منكم وقهر وذل ونفاذ أمر فيهم،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari synthesizes the meanings: the collector’s hand signals dominance and the favor of sparing their lives, while the payer’s hand signals willing submission, direct cash payment, or delivery without an intermediary.
rows.anchor: ولخص الزمخشري في ذلك فقال: إما أن يريد يد الآخذ فمعناه حتى يعلوها عن يد قاهرة مستولية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘While they are humbled’ is a circumstantial clause meaning they are debased and lowly.
rows.anchor: وهم صاغرون جملة حالية أي: ذليلون حقيرون.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they bring the tax in fetters.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يمشون بها ملببين.

rows.speaker: سليمان الفارسي وعكرمة
rows.claim: Salman al-Farsi says payers receive no praise; ʿIkrima says the payer stands while the collector sits.
rows.anchor: وقال سليمان الفارسي: لا يحمدون على إعطائهم. وقال عكرمة: يكون قائما والآخذ جالسا.

rows.speaker: الكلبي والبغوي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi reports the payer is told to pay and struck on the nape; al-Baghawi says he is seized by the beard and struck at the jaw.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: يقال له عند دفعها أد الجزية ويصك في قفاه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explanation that ‘son’ loses tanwīn because it qualifies Uzayr between two proper names is strained; the real objection is the attribution of sonship to God, with an omitted predicate such as ‘our deity.’
rows.anchor: الذي أنكر عليهم إنما هو نسبة البنوة إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘With their mouths’ means an unsupported, empty utterance, like meaningless sounds: meaningful speech also affects the heart, whereas empty speech is only mouth-deep; alternatively the phrase simply emphasizes speech, like ‘write with their hands.’
rows.anchor: أنه قول لا يعضده برهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted object in ‘they imitate’ may be the saying of earlier unbelieving forebears, pagan claims that angels are God’s daughters, or Christian claims about Jesus echoed by Jews about Uzayr; Qatada takes the last comparison and notes Jews predate Christians.
rows.anchor: المشركون القائلون الملائكة بنات الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAsim and Ibn Musarrif read yudāhiʾūn with hamza; the other seven readers read it without one.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وابن مصرف: يضاهئون بالهمز، وباقي السبعة بغير همز.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘May God fight them’ is a general imprecation for every kind of evil; Ibn Abbas glosses it as ‘may He curse them,’ while Qatada glosses it as ‘He killed them.’
rows.anchor: دعاء عليهم عام لأنواع الشر، ومن قاتله الله فهو المقتول.

rows.speaker: أبان بن تغلب
rows.claim: Aban ibn Taghlib cites a poem using qātalahā Allāh in the sense of ‘may God fight her.’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: معناه لعنهم الله.

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري والنقاش
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari glosses the phrase as enmity; al-Naqqash says it began as a prayer but became an exclamation of wonder in good or evil without literal intent.
rows.anchor: وقال أبان بن تغلب: قاتلها الله تلحاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression is not true reciprocal combat but a conventional idiom like ṭāraqt al-naʿl and ʿāqabtu al-liss; the cited al-Asmaʿi poem shows its exclamatory use.
rows.anchor: وليس من باب المفاعلة بل من باب طارقت النعل وعاقبت اللص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘How are they turned away?’ expresses amazement at their turning from the truth after its proof became clear.
rows.anchor: كيف يصرفون عن الحق بعد وضوح الدليل على سبيل التعجب
